lessons.goal: 區分直接引語、改寫與群體立場的歸屬。

questions.evidence: [Review team] Tess: I wrote, 'Everyone found the play confusing.' Is that fair? Omar: I said the opening scene was confusing, but the ending helped me understand it. Pia: I enjoyed it throughout. Please don't turn one comment into the whole group's opinion.
questions.explanation: Omar 只說開頭難懂，結尾幫助了理解。
options: The entire play permanently.
Pia's review.
The opening scene.
The ticket instructions.

questions.evidence: [Review team] Tess: I wrote, 'Everyone found the play confusing.' Is that fair? Omar: I said the opening scene was confusing, but the ending helped me understand it. Pia: I enjoyed it throughout. Please don't turn one comment into the whole group's opinion.
questions.explanation: Pia 意見不同，Omar 的看法也有範圍限制。
options: All three people used identical words.
Only Tess was allowed to comment.
Nobody watched the play.
Pia enjoyed the play and Omar's reaction was limited.

questions.evidence: Tess: I'll write that some viewers needed time to understand the opening. Omar: Can you say that this was my experience? We only asked three people. Pia: And if you quote me, use my actual words. A summary is fine, but it shouldn't look like an exact quotation.
questions.explanation: Pia 要求引用時保留原話。
options: Use her actual words.
Replace her words with Omar's.
Describe the whole class as agreeing.
Remove quotation marks from every review.
questions.prompt: What does Pia request for a direct quote?

questions.evidence: Tess revises the review. She attributes the opening-scene comment to Omar, includes Pia's different reaction, and marks her own summary clearly. The piece now contains disagreement without becoming untidy. Its readers can tell who said what and how much the report supports. Tess learns that making a group sound united can remove information readers need.
questions.explanation: 修訂後清楚將開場評論歸於 Omar。
options: Identifies the person responsible for a statement.
Changes a negative opinion into praise.
Makes a statement longer.
Hides the speaker's identity.

questions.evidence: Tess: I'll write that some viewers needed time to understand the opening. Omar: Can you say that this was my experience? We only asked three people. Pia: And if you quote me, use my actual words. A summary is fine, but it shouldn't look like an exact quotation.

options: It removes the need to report Pia's view.
It makes the review an exact transcript.

questions.prompt: Why is naming Omar better than saying 'some viewers' here?

All reactions are presented as direct quotations.

questions.prompt: What improves in the revised review?

lessons.story:
[Review team] Tess: I wrote, 'Everyone found the play confusing.' Is that fair? Omar: I said the opening scene was confusing, but the ending helped me understand it. Pia: I enjoyed it throughout. Please don't turn one comment into the whole group's opinion.

Tess: I'll write that some viewers needed time to understand the opening. Omar: Can you say that this was my experience? We only asked three people. Pia: And if you quote me, use my actual words. A summary is fine, but it shouldn't look like an exact quotation.

Tess revises the review. She attributes the opening-scene comment to Omar, includes Pia's different reaction, and marks her own summary clearly. The piece now contains disagreement without becoming untidy. Its readers can tell who said what and how much the report supports. Tess learns that making a group sound united can remove information readers need.
lessons.title: Whose Words Are in the Review?
